summary.text: A 30-year-old man with hypertension and morbid obesity (BMI 47) developed presyncope, dizziness, chest tightness and lightheadedness with mid-sternal pain radiating to back/jaw while visiting his monozygotic twin three nights after the brother’s type A dissection repair. He was pale/diaphoretic, with equal pulses and BP 140/90 mmHg. Father had aortic insufficiency and ascending aneurysm treated by valve/aortic replacement.

Immediate ECG suggested inferior STEMI with sinus rhythm and inferior ST elevations; authors report concomitant inferior MI. Baseline troponin 17 ng/L, creatinine 1.27 mg/dL, WBC 13.6 K/mcL, BNP 344 pg/mL and lactate 9.1 mmol/L were reported with reference intervals. Family history prompted CTA before cath-lab transport, confirming root-origin type A dissection involving RCA/brachiocephalic origins and ending in proximal descending thoracic aorta; RCA ostium was occluded with no contrast opacification.

Cardiothoracic surgery recommended esmolol infusion, SBP below 120 mmHg and emergency OR activation. Intraoperative TEE showed root 48 mm and ascending 44 mm dilation/flap. Severe RV and inferior-LV hypokinesia led to RCA saphenous-vein CABG, ascending/hemiarch replacement and aortic-valve resuspension.

Cardiogenic shock required VA-ECMO cannulation on postoperative day 1; AKI required temporary CRRT, with its onset day unspecified. Day 3 washout/sternal closure with TEE showed severe biventricular systolic dysfunction. ECMO turndown/decannulation was tolerated by day 7. Undated postoperative AF required cardioversion, and HIT with superficial left short-saphenous thrombosis was treated with bivalirudin. Extubation and oxygen weaning were achieved by discharge. Coumadin was started; dose, route, exact indication and start time are unreported. CRRT transitioned to intermittent dialysis that was eventually stopped, with normal GFR by month 3 after discharge; dialysis-stop timing relative to discharge is unspecified. Genetic predisposition testing remained ordered/uncompleted; HTAD was a concern rather than a confirmed molecular diagnosis.

evidence.quote: We present the case of a 30-year-old man who presented to the emergency department after an episode of near syncope and was found to have concomitant aortic dissection with inferior myocardial infarction. This case is notable because the patient's twin brother had a repair of Stanford type A aortic dissection just three days prior. The patient underwent an emergent ascending aortic graft and coronary artery bypass graft surgery and recovered after a complex postoperative course.

The patient was visiting his monozygotic twin brother who was recovering in the cardiothoracic intensive care unit from repair of a type A aortic dissection he had undergone three nights prior. While there, the patient began to feel lightheaded and experienced mid-sternal chest pain, radiating to his back and jaw. The patient was emergently transported to the ED. Physical examination was notable for a pale, diaphoretic young person with equal peripheral pulses. Vitals were significant for blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg. His laboratory workup was significant for leukocytosis of 13.6 K/mcL, creatinine of 1.27 mg/dL, baseline troponin of 17 ng/L, lactate of 9.1 mmol/L, and B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) of 344 pg/mL (Table 1). A 12-lead electrocardiogram (EKG) was obtained immediately and suggested an inferior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) (Figure 1).

This case also illustrates the diagnostic challenge of AAD presenting as a STEMI. Our patient arrived with classic inferior ST-segment elevations. Eighty percent of individuals with type A aortic dissection present with chest pain; up to 30% of type A dissections are initially misdiagnosed as another condition, most frequently acute coronary syndrome []. Electrocardiographic changes occur in approximately 20% of AAD presentations, and true STEMI occurs in 4-5%, most often involving the inferior wall, as dissection often occurs along the right lateral wall of the ascending aorta, where the shear stress is high []. In this case, the treatment team's awareness of the patient's strong family history prompted reconsideration before administering antiplatelet or thrombolytic therapy, thereby preventing potentially catastrophic complications.

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Author-stated concomitant inferior MI retained alongside initial ECG suspicion; no obstructive atherosclerotic ACS, serial troponin rise or type 1 mechanism inferred.

evidence.quote: On postoperative day 3, a mediastinal washout with sternal closure was performed in the OR. Intraoperative TEE showed severely reduced systolic function of the LV and RV. By postoperative day 7, the patient tolerated ECMO turndown and was decannulated. Moreover, the postoperative course was complicated by atrial fibrillation requiring cardioversion and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with a superficial left short saphenous vein thrombus for which he was treated with bivalirudin. The patient was successfully extubated and weaned off from oxygen by discharge. Coumadin was started, and he was transitioned to intermittent dialysis, which was eventually discontinued, and the patient had a normal glomerular filtration rate (GFR) by month 3 after discharge. A genetic test was ordered to evaluate the possibility of a genetic predisposition for AAD, but at the time of this case report, the patient had not completed testing.

The strong family history, including aneurysms in the patient's father and brother, raises concern for heritable thoracic aortic disease (HTAD). Modern HTAD gene panels now include more than 30 genes known to confer risk for thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection, encompassing extracellular matrix genes (e.g., FBN1, COL3A1), smooth muscle contractile protein genes (e.g., ACTA2, MYH11, MYLK), and TGF-β signaling genes (e.g., TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD3) []. Although genetic testing was ordered for our patient, there is no documentation that it was completed. The near-simultaneous timing of the dissections in the monozygotic twins should raise the question of whether a timed genetic mechanism exists behind the two occurrences. Additional research is needed to explore this question. Familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection have been associated with a few underlying heritable connective tissue disorders. For example, Marfan syndrome is associated with the mutation of the FBN1 gene that codes for fibrillin-1, a protein in the extracellular matrix [].

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not assign Marfan, FBN1 variant, any listed panel genes or timed genetic mechanism to twins; testing was not completed.

evidence.quote: aneurysms in the patient's father and brother

The patient was visiting his monozygotic twin brother who was recovering in the cardiothoracic intensive care unit from repair of a type A aortic dissection he had undergone three nights prior. While there, the patient began to feel lightheaded and experienced mid-sternal chest pain, radiating to his back and jaw. The patient was emergently transported to the ED. Physical examination was notable for a pale, diaphoretic young person with equal peripheral pulses. Vitals were significant for blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg. His laboratory workup was significant for leukocytosis of 13.6 K/mcL, creatinine of 1.27 mg/dL, baseline troponin of 17 ng/L, lactate of 9.1 mmol/L, and B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) of 344 pg/mL (Table 1). A 12-lead electrocardiogram (EKG) was obtained immediately and suggested an inferior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) (Figure 1).
